opus-5.5.text:
Actually, I think there's a small mix-up. I wasn't at OpenAI. There are two people named Shunyu Yao in AI, and people confuse us all the time. The other Shunyu Yao was at OpenAI. I was at Anthropic, and then I moved to Google DeepMind.

As for why I left Anthropic, it wasn't one single thing. Part of it was that I didn't fully agree with some of the company's views and the way it talks about certain things publicly. That was a real factor, but not all of it. The rest was more personal. I come from physics, and when I joined I wanted to learn how frontier models are actually built and trained. After some time I felt I had learned a lot of what I came to learn, and I wanted to see a different environment and a different way of doing research.

DeepMind appealed to me because it has a deep scientific culture and a broad scope. There's room to think about fundamental questions, not only the next product cycle. So it was partly disagreement and partly curiosity: a sense that it was the right time for my next stage.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the word "leave" makes it sound more dramatic than it felt from the inside. I didn't leave because something was wrong. OpenAI is probably the best place in the world to see what the frontier looks like right now, and I learned an enormous amount there, both about the technology and about how a company at that scale actually makes decisions. I have a lot of respect for the people, Sam included.

The decision was more about where I think the interesting problems are going to be over the next few years, and what kind of role I wanted to play in them.

I wrote an essay called "The Second Half" where I tried to put my view down. The short version is that for most of the last decade, the hard part of AI was the method. How do you train the model, how do you make RL actually work on language, how do you get reasoning to generalize. I think that part is now, roughly, understood. Not finished, but the recipe is there, and a lot of very capable teams are executing on it. Once that's true, the bottleneck shifts. The hard part becomes: what problems do we point these systems at, how do we define them, how do we evaluate them in a way that actually reflects real-world value rather than benchmark saturation, and how do we turn capability into products that people genuinely use.

That's the part I personally find most exciting, and it's also the part where I felt one more researcher at a company that already has thousands of brilliant people might have less marginal impact than I'd like. At a big, mature ship, your job is to make the ship go faster in the direction it's already going. I wanted to be somewhere that's a bit earlier in that curve, where the direction itself is still being figured out, and where I can be closer to the full loop from research to environment to product.

There was also a personal dimension. I'm Chinese, my family is here, and I've watched the ecosystem here change a lot in the last two years. There's a real window right now where the gap in model capability is narrowing and the question of who builds the best agents, the best evaluations, the best applications is genuinely open. I wanted to be part of answering that, rather than watching it from across the ocean.

So I'd frame it less as walking away from something and more as walking toward something. I think the first half of AI was won in a small number of labs in the Bay Area. I'm not sure the second half will be decided in the same place, or by the same kind of work. I wanted to bet on that.
